entries.name: Yangshao culture
entries.region: Yellow River middle reaches (Henan, Shaanxi, Shanxi)
subsistence: early silk hints at Jiahu (Peiligang kin)
entries.settlement: clan villages of pit-houses; Banpo (Xi'an) is the type site
entries.beliefs: ancestor cult; clan burials with grave goods; fish and frog fertility symbolism
entries.fell_by: succeeded by Longshan out of the east; not destroyed, absorbed
entries.notes: The classic Chinese Neolithic: red painted pots with fish and spirals. Good as the game's template for a village-farming tier before bronze.

entries.name: Hongshan culture
entries.region: West Liaoning and eastern Inner Mongolia (Liao River basin)
entries.settlement: dispersed villages around ceremonial centres; Niuheliang temple complex is the type site
monuments: Lady Hao-style jade wealth in tombs (later Shang echo)
trade: regional jade networks across northeast Asia
entries.beliefs: fertility and mother-goddess cult; jade as ceremonial wealth; elaborate mound graves
entries.fell_by: abandoned and faded by c. 2900 BCE; succeeded by Xiaoheyan
entries.notes: The 'dawn of Chinese jade culture'. A goddess temple and jade pig-dragons in the far northeast: spectacular on a world map, and unexpected to most players.

entries.name: Liangzhu culture
entries.region: Yangtze River delta (Zhejiang and Jiangsu)
entries.settlement: walled waterside towns with dams and reservoirs; Mojiaoshan palace centre with peripheral craft villages
monuments: Yaoshan and Fanshan elite cemetery mounds
crafts: jade cong and bi with masked-face designs
trade: jade reaching inland China; its designs echo into Shang bronzes
entries.beliefs: shamanic ancestor cult; jade insignia marked a ruling elite; deciphered as proto-state religion
entries.fell_by: collapse c. 2300 BCE, likely conquest plus floods and climate shift; descendants flowed into early Bronze Age cultures
entries.notes: Often called 'China's first state' in spirit: rice paddies, dams, walls and jade hoards. A watery, delta-flavoured alternative starting point for the south.

entries.name: Longshan culture
entries.region: Yellow River middle and lower reaches (Shanxi, Henan, Shandong)
climate: Dwa/Cfa monsoon, drier in the north
entries.settlement: walled rammed-earth towns; Taosi and Shimao are the giants
monuments: Shimao stone-and-earth wall city (over 4 km long)
crafts: wheel-made eggshell-thin black pottery (gui and jia tripods)
trade: early metal goods entering from the northwest
entries.beliefs: ancestor and sky cults; divination by heated bone; elite feasting as statecraft
entries.fell_by: absorbed by Erlitou and the rise of Shang cities
entries.notes: Copper-age-to-bronze bridge. Shimao's stone-faced walls and Taosi's astronomy make it the natural 'warlord city' tier before Shang bronzes.

entries.name: Erlitou culture
entries.region: Henan-Shanxi border, central China
entries.settlement: palace-centred state capital at Yanshi; roughly 100 ha with grid streets and rammed-earth halls
crafts: bronze jue tripods and ritual wine vessels (China's first full bronzes)
entries.beliefs: proto-Shang ancestor worship; scapulimancy before writing; royal burial rites
entries.fell_by: succeeded by early Shang (Erligang); possibly the memory behind the Xia dynasty
entries.notes: Candidate for the Xia of legend: first palatial capital, first ritual bronzes. A must for any game that wants 'the first city' in China.

entries.name: Sanxingdui (ancient Shu)
entries.region: Chengdu plain, Sichuan basin
entries.settlement: walled city with a ritual precinct (c. 12 sq km site area) around the sacrificial pits
monuments: Sanxingdui sacrificial pits 1 and 2 (and the 2021 finds)
crafts: giant bronze masks and heads (protruding eyes)
trade: copper and tin from Yunnan and the northwest
entries.beliefs: ancestor and mountain-sky cult; giant masks are gods or deified ancestors; no readable script, deliberately destroyed offerings
entries.fell_by: vanished by c. 1150 BCE; Shu culture continued at Jinsha; possibly a convulsion of coups or river shifts
entries.notes: The weird kingdom of Sichuan: 3-metre bronze trees and bulging eyes. Perfect for a secret or ruin biome off the main Silk Road.

entries.name: Shang dynasty
entries.region: North China plain (Henan, Hebei, Shandong); capital at Anyang (Yinxu)
entries.settlement: walled capital that moved repeatedly; Yin (Anyang) is unwalled but planned with palace clusters and royal tombs
monuments: Anyang (Yinxu) ruins and Fu Hao tomb
trade: copper and tin from the south and west
entries.beliefs: Shangdi (the high god) plus hundreds of nature spirits and ancestors; oracle-bone divination for every decision; human and animal sacrifice
entries.fell_by: defeated by Zhou at Muye (1046 BCE); survivors enfeoffed as Song (extinguished 286 BCE)
entries.notes: Bronze, blood and bone script: the Shang writes its name on oracle bones and its ancestors rule the sky. The anchor culture for the Early Bronze Age.

entries.name: Western Zhou dynasty
entries.region: Wei River valley (Shaanxi), then Luoyang after the move east
entries.settlement: fengjian fiefs: walled lordly cities, ancestral temples, and peasant hamlets
monuments: Sanmenxia Guoji (Guo lord) tombs copper inscriptions
entries.beliefs: Mandate of Heaven (Tianming): Heaven grants the throne and may withdraw it; moralized ancestor cult
entries.fell_by: Quanrong nomads sacked Haojing (771 BCE); the court fled east to Luoyang, ending the Western Zhou
entries.notes: The Zhou invented the Mandate of Heaven to justify replacing the Shang: every later Chinese dynasty inherits this rulebook.

entries.name: Warring States (Eastern Zhou)
entries.region: all of China, seven major states (Qin, Chu, Qi, Yan, Zhao, Wei, Han)
entries.settlement: vast walled capitals (Linzi, Handan); beginnings of the tianxia interstate system
trade: silk, lacquer and grain between states
controversial roads and canals (Jian River link)
entries.beliefs: the Hundred Schools: Confucianism, Daoism, Mohism, Legalism, Logicians and Yin-Yang; 'a hundred flowers' of argument
entries.fell_by: Qin conquered the states one by one, 230-221 BCE
entries.notes: The intellectual big bang: Confucius is earlier (Spring and Autumn), but Warring States made the arguments that still structure Chinese thought.

entries.name: Qin dynasty
entries.region: Guanzhong (Shaanxi) heartland, then the whole unified realm
entries.settlement: all-China commandery (jun) and county system; Xianyang (near modern Xi'an) as planned capital
crafts: standardized weights, measures, coin (ban liang) and axle width
trade: standardized currency finally made exchange mechanical
entries.beliefs: Legalist state cult; Five Elements (wuxing) cosmology as state ideology; ancestor cult suppressed in favour of the state
entries.fell_by: rebellions after Qin Shi Huang's death (210 BCE); fell in 206 BCE to Liu Bang of Han
entries.notes: Fifteen years of total empire: one script, one axle, one wall. The name 'China' itself derives from Qin.

entries.name: Han dynasty (Western and Eastern)
entries.region: China proper; Chang'an (2nd c BCE) then Luoyang (1st-2nd c CE)
entries.settlement: commandery-county grid; Chang'an and Luoyang as walled grid cities with market wards
crafts: paper (Cai Lun credited 105 CE; archaeology shows older paper)
trade: silk and lacquer west on the Silk Road
entries.beliefs: Huang-Lao Daoism early, then state Confucianism (Han Wudi, 141 BCE); Five Elements cosmology; heaven-human resonance
entries.fell_by: warlords after the Yellow Turban revolt (184 CE); split into Three Kingdoms (220 CE)
entries.notes: The dynasty that gave the majority Chinese people their name: 'Han people' means 'of the Han'. Model the Silk Road here.

entries.name: Northern Wei (Tuoba Xianbei)
entries.region: Datong, then Luoyang (from 494 CE)
entries.settlement: sinicized royal capitals; Datong then a rebuilt Luoyang filled with Buddhist temples
entries.beliefs: Buddhism as imperial religion (patronage of grottoes) plus Daoism and Confucian ritual; Xianbei shamanic roots underneath
entries.fell_by: split into Eastern and Western Wei (534/535); absorbed into Northern Zhou and Sui
entries.notes: Nomad conquerors who chose Chinese culture wholesale: moved the capital, banned Xianbei dress, rebuilt Luoyang. A fascinating sinicization case.

entries.name: Tang dynasty
entries.region: China proper; Chang'an (Xi'an) and Luoyang, with protectorates to Xinjiang and Annam
subsistence: tea spreading after Lu Yu's Cha jing (760)
entries.settlement: Chang'an, the largest city on Earth (~1 million people): walled grid of 108 wards; Luoyang second capital
monuments: Zhaoling (Taizong's tomb with carved stone horses)
crafts: regulated verse poetry (Li Bai, Du Fu, Wang Wei)
trade: spices, glass, ivory and horses in
Chang'an full of Persians, Arabs, Sogdians and Japanese monks
entries.beliefs: the Three Religions (Buddhism, Daoism, Confucianism) coexisting; state cult of Heaven; Buddhism at imperial high water
entries.fell_by: An Lushan rebellion (755-763) crippled the court; last Tang abdicated 907; Five Dynasties chaos
entries.notes: The golden age players expect: poetry, polo, cosmopolitan Chang'an. The peak example of openness before Chinese seclusion set in.

entries.name: Liao dynasty (Khitan)
entries.region: Manchuria and the north; capital at Linhuang (Balinzuo) with Nanjing (modern Beijing) as secondary capital
subsistence: millet and wheat in the south ('dual administration')
entries.settlement: five capitals with dual administration: Khitan law in the north, Chinese-style prefectures in the south
monuments: Yingxian wooden pagoda (1056, tallest all-wood tower on Earth)
trade: silk and grain from Song (the 'Shanyuan treaty' tribute-in-reverse, 1004)
entries.beliefs: Buddhism (imperial) + Khitan shamanism + Confucian scholarship for the south
entries.fell_by: conquered by the Jurchen Jin (1120-1125); remnants fled west as the Kara Khitai (1124-1218)
entries.notes: The Khitan invented 'dual administration': ride with the horsemen, file with the bureaucrats. Beijing's political debut as a capital.

entries.name: Song dynasty (Northern and Southern)
entries.region: Kaifeng (960-1127), then Hangzhou (1127-1279) south of the Yangzi
climate: Cfa/Dwa monsoon; drenching monsoon rice south
subsistence: double-cropped rice in the Pearl and Yangzi deltas
entries.settlement: open-walled market cities; Kaifeng then Hangzhou (roughly a million each): night markets, bridges, floating restaurants
crafts: gunpowder weapons (fire arrows and early cannon by 1100s)
Ru, Guan, Ge, Jun and Ding porcelain
trade: porcelain, silk and tea out by sea (Quanzhou, Mingzhou/Ningbo)
entries.beliefs: Neo-Confucianism forming (Zhou Dunyi, Cheng Hao/Yi, later Zhu Xi); Chan Buddhism widespread; literati culture; Mazu cult takes root on the coast
entries.fell_by: Jurchen Jin took Kaifeng (1127); Mongols took Hangzhou (1276) and crushed the last fleet at Yaishan (1279)
entries.notes: Arguably the world's first commercial and industrial society: paper money, gunpowder, movable type, million-person cities. The banker-and-engineer era.

entries.name: Western Xia (Tangut)
entries.region: Ningxia and the Hexi corridor; capital at Xingqing (Yinchuan)
climate: BWk cold desert with Yellow River irrigation
subsistence: camel caravans taxing the Silk Road
entries.settlement: desert fortress cities with Tangut court culture; Helan mountains full of imperial tombs
crafts: Tangut script woodblock printing (massive imperial editions)
trade: Silk Road tolls between Song and Liao/Jin
entries.beliefs: Buddhism dominant: Tibetan Vajrayana at court and Chinese Chan among the people
entries.fell_by: destroyed by Genghis Khan (1209) and finished under Emperor Xizong (1227); the Tangut people and language went fully extinct by the 1500s
entries.notes: The only fully extinct Chinese dynasty and script. A vanished civilization is catnip for a game: secret libraries, dead languages, sand-covered pyramids.

entries.name: Jin dynasty (Jurchen)
entries.region: Manchuria, then north China from Zhongdu (Beijing, 1153)
subsistence: millet and wheat in north China (after conquest)
entries.settlement: dual administration again: Jurchen hunting-camp law for the north, Chinese prefectures in the south; Zhongdu as capital
monuments: Zhongdu (Beijing's Yuan/Ming predecessor) and its Marco Polo Bridge (Lugou qiao, 1192)
trade: silk and grain from the former Song north
curio trade with Song (peace by treaty, 1141)
entries.beliefs: Jurchen shamanism (gods of earth and mountains) underneath a Confucian-Buddhist official culture
entries.fell_by: Mongol conquest, 1211-1234; the last Jin emperor committed suicide as Caizhou fell
entries.notes: The ancestor of the Manchu. The Jurchen wrote their own script, then chose Han culture for the south: a template for conquest-dynasty tension.

entries.name: Yuan dynasty (Mongol)
entries.region: all China plus Mongolia; capital at Dadu (Beijing)
entries.settlement: Dadu, a grid capital planned by Liu Bingzhong; Karakorum earlier; Quanzhou the great southern port
monuments: Dadu (Yuan palace, later buried under the Forbidden City)
Xanadu (Shangdu), the summer capital of Coleridge fame
crafts: blue-and-white porcelain (Jingdezhen, using imported Persian cobalt)
paper currency (chao, collapses into chaos later)
trade: Quanzhou: the busiest port on Earth in 1300
silk and porcelain to Persia and beyond (Marco Polo, Ibn Battuta)
entries.beliefs: Tibetan Buddhism as the imperial cult (the Sakya lama as 'state preceptor'); shamanism among Mongols; Islam in the northwest; Confucian exam reinstated 1313
entries.fell_by: Red Turban revolts; Zhu Yuanzhang took Dadu (1368); Mongol remnants fled north (the Northern Yuan, 1368-1635)
entries.notes: The empire that welded China into Eurasia. Marco Polo walked in; so did bubonic plague, eventually: pick what the game wants from this door opening.

entries.name: Ming dynasty
entries.region: China proper; Nanjing (1368-1421) then Beijing (from 1421)
subsistence: maize, sweet potato, peanut and tobacco arrive from the Americas (c. 1550-1600)
entries.settlement: Beijing with the Forbidden City (1406-1420); every county town walled; Nanjing the southern second capital
monuments: great_wall_of_china (brick rebuild as we see it)
Zheng He's fleet docks at Nanjing Longjiang
crafts: blue-and-white porcelain at its peak (xuande, chenghua 'chicken-cup')
trade: porcelain and silk to Malacca, India, Hormuz and the Swahili coast
silver in (Spanish and Japanese mines) - the silver century
entries.beliefs: Confucian state cult (civil service exam in full force) plus popular folk religion (Mazu, Guan Yu, City God cults); Chan and Pure Land Buddhism thrived
entries.fell_by: Li Zicheng's rebels took Beijing (1644); the last Ming loyalists (Southern Ming) crushed by 1662; pirate-war and climate strains all along
entries.notes: The porcelain-and-seapower dynasty: China could have had an ocean age in 1405, then chose walls. A hinge moment for any history-based game.

entries.name: Qing dynasty (Manchu)
entries.region: China proper plus Tibet, Xinjiang, Mongolia and Taiwan; capital Beijing
subsistence: New World staples spread: maize, sweet potato, potato, peanut (1700s) fed a tripled population
entries.settlement: Beijing (Manchu banner city-within-city); Mukden palace in Shenyang; Chinese county towns with banner garrisons
monuments: Old Summer Palace (Yuanmingyuan, sacked 1860, ruins kept)
crafts: silk and tea for the European market
trade: tea and porcelain out; silver in - then opium in, silver out (the Opium Wars)
the Canton system: one port (Guangzhou), one season
entries.beliefs: Confucian orthodoxy (Kangxi-Yongzheng-Qianlong as 'sage kings'); Tibetan Buddhism patronized for legitimacy; Manchu imperial shamanism; Christianity suppressed (after 1724)
entries.fell_by: Xinhai Revolution (1911); abdication of Puyi, 12 February 1912
entries.notes: The Manchu made China the biggest it has ever been, then lost it in a century of gunboats. The queue hairstyle was the price of submission - a visceral game hook.

entries.name: Han Chinese
entries.region: all of China proper, plus vast diaspora (Southeast Asia, Americas, Europe)
entries.era: Huaxia roots c. 2000 BCE; the name 'Han' from 202 BCE - now
entries.settlement: villages and market towns; northern siheyuan courtyards; southern clustered townhouses along rivers
trade: silk, tea, porcelain out along every route (overland and maritime)
silver, spices and silver-borne goods in
entries.beliefs: folk religion (Mazu, City God, kitchen god) plus Buddhism and Daoism; Confucian ethics; clan and ancestor halls
entries.notes: The world's largest ethnic group (well over a billion). Not a costume but the main stage: every Chinese dynasty above is 'theirs'.

entries.name: Cantonese (Yue people)
entries.region: Pearl River Delta (Guangdong and Hong Kong/Macau); diaspora in Southeast Asia and the West
climate: Cwa/Cfa subtropical monsoon, wet and hot
entries.settlement: delta towns and walled villages; Cantonese emigrant towers (Kaiping diaolou); Hong Kong as world port
trade: maritime trade from Guangzhou for 2000 years
emigrant remittances (the 'Money Mountain' of the 19th century)
perishable goods and later manufacturing exports
entries.beliefs: folk religion especially Tianhou (goddess of the sea); Buddhism; strong clan-lineage halls (citang); Tanka water-cults
entries.notes: The sailors and shopkeepers of China's age of sail: Cantonese is the sound of old Chinatowns everywhere from San Francisco to Yokohama.

entries.name: Hakka (Kejia) people
entries.region: southeast Fujian, Jiangxi, Guangdong hills; wide diaspora in Taiwan, SE Asia and the West
entries.era: c. 4th-13th c CE migrations (from north China) - now
entries.settlement: clan mountain villages; roundhouse tulou (Fujian) and weilongwu (Guangdong) as fortress-homes
trade: Hakka as frugal merchant and teacher class
entries.beliefs: folk religion and ancestor worship; famed lineage halls; Christian converts common in the 19th century (Hakka Christians disproportionate)
entries.notes: The 'guest people': five migrations south in a thousand years, each time fortifying. Tulou are literal fortress apartment buildings for 80 families.

entries.name: Hui Chinese (Chinese-speaking Muslims)
entries.region: Ningxia, Gansu, Qinghai core; scattered communities in every province (Xi'an, Kunming)
entries.era: c. 7th-10th c CE (Tang-Yuan-era Muslim communities) - now
climate: Dwa/BWk northwest; the whole monsoon range nationwide
subsistence: tea, horse and salt caravan trade (historical)
entries.settlement: market towns and city Muslim quarters; Ningxia oasis villages; Xi'an Muslim Street (Beiyuanmen)
monuments: Great Mosque of Xi'an (Huajue Lane, Ming era, Chinese-style mosque)
trade: caravan goods (tea, salt, horses, furs) across the steppe edge
silk and ceramics with Central Asia
entries.beliefs: Sunni Islam (Hanafi), practiced in Chinese; Quranic schools (jingtang jiaoyu); halal cuisine as daily identity
entries.notes: Muslims fluent in Chinese culture: the Xi'an mosque looks like a Confucian temple with a minaret hidden inside. Lived Islam wearing Han clothes.

entries.name: Zhuang people
entries.region: Guangxi (and borderlands of Yunnan, Guizhou, Hunan, Guangdong); the largest minority in China
subsistence: paddy rice (karst valley paddies and ledges)
entries.settlement: karst stone villages; Zuojiang rock-art country (200+ cliff faces); stilt and stone houses
trade: local markets: rice, herbs, lime, timber
tea-horse and Great South gate routes
entries.beliefs: folk religion plus the Buluotuo epic (a Zhuang genesis sung at festivals); ancestor and river-spirit cults; 麽 shamanism in older sources

examples: Nong Zhigao (11th c king of Nan Dan, rebel against Song)

entries.notes: Twenty million people the average player has never heard of. Their cliff paintings in the Zuojiang gorge are 2,000 years of painted festivals.

entries.name: Tibetans (Bod pa)
entries.region: Tibetan plateau: Xizang (TAR), Qinghai, and western Sichuan (Ganzi, Aba) and NW Yunnan (Diqing)
entries.era: c. 500 BCE (proto-Tibetan tribes); Tibetan empire from 629 CE - now
climate: ET alpine plateau (four thousand metres up)
subsistence: yaks and dzo (milk, butter, meat, transport)
salt for grain trade (the salt road)
wheat and buckwheat in river valleys
entries.settlement: monasteries as towns (Labrang, Sera, Drepung); fortified dzong towns; nomad black-hair-tent camps
trade: tea-horse road (tea in, war horses out, until 1912)
salt, wool and yak tails out; tea, grain and cloth in
entries.beliefs: Tibetan Buddhism (Gelug, Kagyu, Nyingma, Sakya) layered over Bon (shamanic) roots; prayer flags, prayer wheels, sky burial; lamas as teachers and rulers
entries.notes: Plateau civilization at 4,000 metres: yak pastoralism, barley bread, and monasteries the size of towns. Sky burial is real and a big design question.

entries.name: Uyghurs
entries.region: Xinjiang: Tarim and Junggar basins (Kashgar, Hotan, Turpan, Aksu, Ili)
entries.era: 840 CE (Uyghurs settle Turfan after the Khaganate's fall) - now
climate: extreme continental (Turpan - below sea level, 48°C summers)
subsistence: oasis agriculture: grapes, melons (Hami melon!), cotton, wheat and maize
entries.settlement: oasis cities with grand bazaars: Kashgar's id Kah, Turpan, Hotan; flat-roofed mud-brick houses
monuments: Jiaohe and Gaochang ruined Silk Road capitals
trade: Silk Road heartland: jade (Hotan), horses, dried fruit, cotton and carpets out
the bazaars bridged China, Persia and the steppe
entries.beliefs: Sunni Islam (Hanafi); before Islam: Buddhism, Manichaeism (Uyghurs were Manichaean evangelists) and Nestorian Christianity

examples: Mahmud al-Kashgari (author of the first Turkic encyclopaedia, 1070)
Yusuf Khass Hajib (author of the Kutadgu Bilig, 1070)

entries.notes: The Far East's caravan-city culture: melons in the desert, minarets in the sand, and a linguistic tradition as old as Runic Turkic.

entries.name: Yi people (Lolo)
entries.region: mountainous Liangshan (Sichuan), Chuxiong and Honghe (Yunnan), western Guizhou
subsistence: sheep, goats and horses (Yi are famously horse keepers)
entries.settlement: mountain villages on ridgelines; clan (wu-zhi) settlements; historically walled villages against Han encroachment
monuments: Stone Forest (Shilin) is Sani (closely related) county
crafts: Yi lacquerware (painted black/red wooden vessels and figures)
bimo script manuscripts (classical Yi, still used by shamans)
trade: horses to Sichuan and Yunnan fairs (the horse trade sustained Yi power for centuries)
entries.beliefs: Bimo shamanism: literate priests (bimo) keep genealogies and perform exorcisms; ancestor cult; earth, sky and fire gods
entries.notes: A slave-holding mountain aristocracy into the 1950s, literate in its own syllabary: the Yi are China's great 'other highlanders'.

entries.name: Naxi people
entries.region: Lijiang (Yunnan) and Shangri-La (NW Yunnan); small communities in Sichuan (Muli) and Tibet
entries.era: c. 700 CE (Moxie in Tang records); Naxi tusi rule 1270s-1723 - now
entries.settlement: Dayan (Old Town of Lijiang, UNESCO 1997): Naxi townhouses around canals, with carved beams and painted frescoes
monuments: Mu palace (Mu Fu) of the Naxi tusi
trade: tea-horse road: muleteer caravans linking Yunnan to Tibet and India
entries.beliefs: Dongba religion (shamanic; the last living pictographic religion on Earth) overlaid with Tibetan Buddhism and Daoism; Sandu (three sages) cult

examples: Mu Zeng (Ming-era tusi of Lijiang, scholar-general)

entries.notes: The last living pictographic faith: dongba priests still draw the script today. A village museum of a lost way of writing.

entries.name: Bai people
entries.region: Dali and Erhai basin (western Yunnan), with communities in Sichuan and elsewhere
entries.era: c. 4th c CE (Nanzhao 738-902; Dali kingdom 937-1253) - now
climate: Cwa subtropical Erhai basin (2,000 m plateau)
entries.settlement: Erhai lake towns: Dali (Three Pagodas), Xiaguan, Xizhou; white-walled courtyard villages
monuments: Dali old town and city wall
crafts: Dali marble carving (the 'marble' of Dali is the town's name)
trade: salt from the Tea-Horse Road caravan trade
entries.beliefs: Benzhu (patron-deity) folk religion overlaid with Mahayana and Nanzhao-Dali-era Buddhism; temples on Cangshan mountain's slopes
entries.notes: Ruled by their own kingdom (Nanzhao, then Dali) for 500 years: a real Yunnan state before the Mongols, with Bai kings and a Buddhist court.

entries.name: Miao (Hmong) people
entries.region: Guizhou, Hunan, Yunnan, Guangxi, Sichuan and Chongqing mountains; diaspora in SE Asia and the US
entries.settlement: ridge-top villages strung along mountain spines; ceremonial drum grounds (guichang pingba)
monuments: Xijiang Qianhu Miao village (Guizhou, modern revival)
crafts: silver jewelry headdresses (horn-shaped and sunburst types)
trade: embroidered cloth and silver to local markets
entries.beliefs: folk religion: ancestor cult and village nature spirits; some Miao/Hmong are Christian (especially the US diaspora); festival drum rituals
entries.notes: The great persecuted highlanders: pushed south by every Chinese expansion, now in eight provinces plus a diaspora that changed American demographics.

entries.name: Dai people (Tai Yai)
entries.region: Xishuangbanna and Dehong (southern Yunnan); relatives across the Mekong into Laos, Myanmar and Thailand
entries.era: ancient (Tai migrations c. 0 BCE-1000 CE) - now
climate: Aw tropical monsoon (Yunnan's only true tropics)
entries.settlement: stilt-house villages in bamboo groves; Jingzhen-style clusters; temple (wat) at each village centre
monuments: Manting Park (Jinghong, former royal garden of Cheli)
trade: Mekong border trade (rubber, fruit, rice) with Laos and Myanmar
Pu'er tea from the wider region
entries.beliefs: Theravada Buddhism (village temples, rain-retreat ordinations) layered over water-spirit and ancestor cults; spirit mediums (mo)
entries.notes: China's little piece of Thailand: Water Festival in April, stilt houses, Theravada monks. The southernmost edge of the Chinese world.

entries.name: Dong people
entries.region: southeast Guizhou (Qiandongnan), west Hunan (Xiangxi), north Guangxi (Sanjiang)
entries.era: c. 500 CE (recorded by Tang-Song sources as 'Liao') - now
subsistence: paddy rice (mountain terraces and valley floors)
fish (field-fish culture, paddies stocked with carp)
entries.settlement: river-valley village clusters around drum towers; linked by covered 'wind-and-rain' bridges
monuments: Zhaoxing Dong village ('the biggest Dong village in China')
crafts: master carpentry (drum towers, wind-and-rain bridges - no nails)
indigo and resist-dyed textiles (grandma's mountain flowers)
entries.beliefs: folk religion: nature and ancestor cults, feng shui; some Dong are Christian (Miao-Dong highlanders); song as prayer (the grand song)
entries.notes: Their 'grand song' (Kam grand chorus) is UNESCO-listed, sung polyphonically with no conductor and no written music. Music is how Dong do history.

entries.name: Manchu people
entries.region: Manchuria: Liaoning, Jilin, Heilongjiang; Banner descendants also in Beijing and beyond
entries.era: Jurchen roots ancient; as Manchu c. 1600 - now
entries.settlement: banner towns (Three Eastern Provinces) plus the Manchu Eight Banners inside Beijing (Inner City)
monuments: Yonghe Gong Lamasery (Beijing, Qing imperial monastery)
crafts: sinew-back racing bows (Manchu archery was ruinously accurate)
Manchu-language printing (one of the Qing's lost arts)
trade: sea otter and sable via the Amur
entries.beliefs: Manchu shamanism (imperial, with clan spirit sacrifices) plus Confucian and Buddhist official culture; the emperor sacrificed to Heaven at the Temple of Heaven

examples: Nurhaci (united the Jurchen, founding the Aisin Gioro clan)

entries.notes: Ten million people who conquered China, imposed the queue, ruled it 268 years, and were nearly sinicized out of existence - but their bows conquered it first.

entries.name: Mosuo (Na) people
entries.region: Lugu Lake (Sichuan-Yunnan border, Ninglang and Yanyuan counties)
entries.era: ancient (Na groups recorded in Tang sources) - now
climate: Cwa plateau valley (2,700 m) with alpine lakes
subsistence: fishing (carp and loach in Lugu Lake)
entries.settlement: lakeside hamlets with 'grand houses' (zuwumifang) arranged around a central pillar room
crafts: salt production (historic brine wells around the lake)
trade: pigs, cattle, dried fish and wool to local markets
entries.beliefs: Daba religion (native shamanism with a living priest class) overlaid with Tibetan Buddhism (Chinese-Tibetan frontier monasteries)
entries.notes: Famous for 'walking marriage' (zouhun): couples never live together, and descent is purely maternal. The classic 'kingdom of women' - handle with care and respect.

entries.name: Qiang people
entries.region: Min River gorges of northwest Sichuan (Maoxian, Songpan, Wenchuan, Beichuan); small Qiang communities elsewhere
entries.era: c. 1200 BCE (named in Shang oracle bones) - now
climate: Dwb/ET high mountain gorges and plateau edges
subsistence: highland terrace maize, potatoes and buckwheat
walnuts, Chinese toon (xiangchun) and medicinal herbs
entries.settlement: stone villages strung along gorge walls; the watchtower (diaotounang / qianglou) above each village
crafts: Qiang embroidery (sheep, ram and fish patterns)
stone watchtower and drystone house building
entries.beliefs: white-stone worship: the Qiang keep a shrine of white stones (Baixangshen, the white stone god) on rooftops and cliffs
entries.notes: Oracle bones name them; 2,000 watchtower ruins remember them. Survivors of the 512 Wenchuan earthquake (2008) rebuilt every stone tower by hand.
